nodes.name: Turing machine
nodes.statement: A Turing machine is a finite table of rules that reads and writes symbols on an unbounded tape. It models any step-by-step procedure.

nodes.name: Church-Turing thesis
nodes.statement: The Church-Turing thesis holds that every function computable by an effective step-by-step procedure is computable by a Turing machine.

nodes.name: Programs as data
nodes.statement: Every Turing machine can be written down as a finite string of symbols. So one program can take another program's code as its input.

nodes.name: Universal machine
nodes.statement: A universal Turing machine U takes the code of a machine M and an input x, then simulates M on x step by step.

nodes.name: Halting problem
nodes.statement: The halting problem asks for one procedure that, given any program P and input x, answers in finite time whether P eventually halts on x.

nodes.name: Assumed decider H
nodes.statement: The classic proof assumes, for contradiction, a machine H that always halts and answers yes exactly when program P halts on input x.

nodes.name: The machine D
nodes.statement: From H, one can build a machine D that takes a program P and runs H on P with P's own code as input. D then loops forever if H says yes and halts if H says no.

nodes.name: D run on itself
nodes.statement: Run on its own code, D halts exactly when H reports that D does not halt on its own code.

nodes.name: The contradiction
nodes.statement: If H is correct, then D halts on its own code exactly when it does not. That is impossible, so no such H exists.

nodes.name: Halting is undecidable
nodes.statement: No Turing machine decides the halting problem for all programs and inputs.

nodes.name: No algorithm anywhere
nodes.statement: Given the Church-Turing thesis, no algorithm in any programming language decides the halting problem.

nodes.name: Cantor's diagonal argument
nodes.statement: No list of infinite binary sequences contains every such sequence. Flipping the n-th digit of the n-th sequence, for every n, gives a sequence missing from the list.

nodes.name: Countably many programs
nodes.statement: There are only countably many Turing machines, because each one is a finite string over a finite alphabet.

nodes.name: Uncountably many problems
nodes.statement: There are uncountably many sets of strings, because each set matches an infinite binary sequence of yes and no answers.

nodes.name: Most problems are undecidable
nodes.statement: Most sets of strings have no Turing machine that decides them, since there are far more sets than machines.

nodes.name: Halting is recognizable
nodes.statement: The halting problem is semi-decidable, which means some program answers yes on every halting pair. A universal machine does this by simulating P on x, but it runs forever on pairs that never halt.

nodes.name: Two recognizers decide
nodes.statement: A set is decidable when both it and its complement are semi-decidable, because running both recognizers side by side always ends with one of them answering.

nodes.name: Non-halting is unrecognizable
nodes.statement: The set of program and input pairs that never halt is not even semi-decidable.

nodes.name: Timeouts settle nothing
nodes.statement: Running a program for any fixed number of steps cannot settle halting in general, because a program that has not halted yet may still halt later.

nodes.name: Reduction method
nodes.statement: If a decider for problem B would yield a decider for problem A, and A is undecidable, then B is undecidable too.

nodes.name: Blank-tape halting
nodes.statement: Deciding whether a program halts when started on an empty input is undecidable, because a decider for it would decide the general halting problem.

nodes.name: Rice's theorem
nodes.statement: Every non-trivial property of the function a program computes is undecidable. Non-trivial means some programs have the property and some do not.

nodes.name: Program equivalence
nodes.statement: Deciding whether two programs compute the same function is undecidable. A decider for it could test whether a program matches one that never halts, which is a non-trivial property.

nodes.name: Reaching an error line
nodes.statement: Deciding whether a program ever reaches a given error line is undecidable. Placing that line wherever the program would halt turns a halting question into this one.

nodes.name: Limits of static analysis
nodes.statement: Every static analyzer for a non-trivial program behavior either reports some false alarms, misses some real bugs, or fails to answer on some programs.

nodes.name: Busy beaver
nodes.statement: The busy beaver number BB(n) is the most steps any halting n-state Turing machine takes from a blank tape. BB is not computable, because knowing BB(n) would let a universal machine decide blank-tape halting for n-state machines.

nodes.name: Link to incompleteness
nodes.statement: No consistent, computably axiomatized theory that includes basic arithmetic proves every true statement of the form “P never halts”. Listing its proofs would otherwise make non-halting semi-decidable.
